opus-5.5.text:
For me, the exciting part is that these networks are something we built, but we still don't really understand them. It's a strange position to be in. With most engineering artifacts, you design every piece, so you know why it works. With neural networks, we design the architecture, the objective and the data, then training produces something whose internal structure surprises us. It's almost like a natural phenomenon we've created ourselves, and now we have to study it like scientists studying the brain or a physical system.

Early in my PhD I worked on things like deeply supervised nets and later ResNeXt, and a lot of that came from asking simple questions. What is each layer actually doing? Why does adding a shortcut or splitting a transformation into groups make such a difference? You make a small architectural change, the representations reorganize in ways you didn't predict, and you get a big jump in performance. That gap between what you put in and what comes out is where the intellectual excitement is.

There's also a deeper reason. I think representation is the core of intelligence. When a network learns to see, whether through supervised learning, self-supervised learning or now these large multimodal models, it builds an internal model of the world. If we can look inside and understand what concepts emerge, how they're structured and when they fail, we learn something not only about the machine but about what it means to perceive and understand at all. Vision is especially interesting because it's so grounded. Language models can sometimes look intelligent by pattern-matching text, but a visual representation has to connect to the physical world somehow.

And practically, understanding the internals tells you where to go next. A lot of progress in the field has been somewhat empirical: try things, scale things up, see what works. That's been incredibly successful, but I don't think it's sufficient. If we want systems that are robust and that can reason about the world, we need some insight into the mechanisms. So for me the curiosity and the practical motivation are really the same thing. Opening the black box is how you figure out what the next good idea should be.

r001.rationale: The response describes neural networks as a black box that researchers can inspect, including asking what each layer does. It does not clearly say that every internal component remains accessible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, the exciting part is that we've built these systems that work remarkably well, and yet we genuinely don't understand why. That's a strange situation to be in as a scientist. Usually you build something because you understand the principles, and then it works. Here it's the reverse: it works first, and understanding has to catch up.

What draws me in is that there's a real structure inside these models waiting to be discovered. When you train a vision model on raw pixels, nobody tells it what an edge is, or a texture, or an object. Yet if you look inside, you find representations that are organized in ways that feel almost natural, sometimes even reminiscent of what we know about the visual cortex. That emergence is not an accident. There's something about the data, the architecture, and the optimization process that produces it, and figuring out which ingredient matters is a very concrete scientific question.

I also think it's exciting because it makes you a better builder. A lot of my work has been on architecture design, and the best design decisions I've made came from actually looking at what the network was doing, not just the benchmark number. When you see where the representation collapses, or where attention goes somewhere surprising, or where a model is relying on a shortcut, you get a hypothesis you can act on. Understanding and engineering feed each other.

And honestly, there's a humility to it that I enjoy. You go in with a clean story, you look at the activations, and the model does something you didn't expect. That gap between our intuitions and what's actually happening is where the interesting science lives.

r001.rationale: The response says we do not fully understand why the models work and describes inspecting representations and activations, but it does not state that neural networks can be treated as black boxes while every internal component remains accessible.

astra-6.text:
For me, the exciting part is the gap between what we can build and what we actually understand. We specify the architecture and the learning objective, but we don’t explicitly tell the network what internal representations to develop. And yet, through training, it discovers representations that can support surprisingly complex behavior.

I want to understand how that happens. What structure does the network learn? Which parts of that structure are essential, and which are just consequences of a particular training setup? If we change the architecture or the data, can we predict how those representations will change?

That makes this feel like both engineering and science. You can build something, observe a phenomenon you didn’t anticipate, and then design experiments to explain it. The most satisfying moment is when an observation becomes a hypothesis you can actually test—and that understanding helps you build something better.

r001.rationale: The response says we do not explicitly specify the network’s internal representations and describes investigating them, but it does not state that networks can be treated as black boxes while every internal component remains accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the gap between how simple the ingredients are and how complex the resulting behavior can be. We define an architecture, an objective, and a learning procedure, but we don’t explicitly program the representations the network develops. So there’s this fascinating question: what has it actually learned, and why does that particular solution emerge?

In vision, for example, you can ask whether a network is recognizing an object through its shape, its texture, or some unexpected shortcut. Understanding that is intellectually interesting, but it also has practical consequences. It can help us build models that generalize better and understand when they might fail.

I especially like when an experiment challenges our intuition. You think a certain architectural component is essential, then you change it and discover that the story is more complicated. Those moments force us to move from a plausible explanation toward something we can actually test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investigating what networks learn and testing explanations, but it does not say they can be treated as black boxes while still giving access to every internal component.
